KJV Vocabulary
KAY-JAY-VEE VOK-ab-yoo-lair-ee
n. phrase (biblical languages; textual tradition; biblical literacy)
From KJV (King James Version, the Authorized Version of 1611; commissioned by King James I of England) and Latin vocabularium (a list of words, a word-stock; from vocabulum, a name, a word; from vocare, to call, to name); the distinctive English vocabulary of the King James Bible — its Elizabethan and Jacobean word-forms, its rendering conventions for Hebrew and Greek terms, and its theological lexicon that has shaped English-speaking Christianity's perception of Scripture for four centuries.

Biblical Definition

The vocabulary of the King James Version is not merely archaic English but a theologically shaped translation tradition that makes specific choices about how Hebrew and Greek concepts enter English Christian discourse. Psalm 119:89 declares the permanence of the word the KJV translates: “Forever, O LORD, Your word is settled in heaven.” The Authorized Version was commissioned not to replace previous English Bibles (Tyndale, Coverdale, Geneva) but to produce a faithful common-language Bible authorized for public use — its scholarship involving fifty-four translators in six companies over several years. Proverbs 30:5 provides the standard the translators held themselves to: “Every word of God is pure; He is a shield to those who put their trust in Him.” The KJV's consistent use of “lovingkindness” for Hebrew chesed, “propitiation” for Greek hilastērion, “sanctification” for hagiasmos, and “justification” for dikaiosis embedded a Reformed soteriological vocabulary into common English use. Isaiah 40:8 anchors the confidence underlying the translation project: “the word of our God stands forever.” Christ's own promise in Matthew 24:35 confirms the ultimate ground: “Heaven and earth will pass away — but My words shall not pass away.” The KJV vocabulary is the English translation tradition's most enduring contribution to Christian literacy — not because the 1611 text is inspired but because its specific lexical choices have shaped four centuries of English-speaking Christian thought, hymnody, preaching, and confession.

Webster 1828 Definition

KJV vocabulary designates the English theological lexicon of the 1611 Authorized Version — its specific rendering choices for Hebrew and Greek that shaped Reformed theological language across four centuries, embedded in hymnody, confessions, and pastoral discourse, preserving in English the doctrinal precision the translators carried from the Received Text.

KJV VOCABULARY, n. phrase (biblical languages; textual tradition). The distinctive English word-stock of the King James Authorized Version of 1611: its Elizabethan and Jacobean word-forms, its rendering conventions for Hebrew and Greek theological terms, and its lexical decisions that shaped English-speaking Christianity's doctrinal perception of Scripture for four hundred years.

The KJV's translators stood in the tradition of William Tyndale (d. 1536), whose early sixteenth-century New Testament translation established many of the key English equivalents the KJV inherited: repentance (for Greek metanoia), congregation (for ekklesia, though the KJV standardized “church”), elder (for presbyteros), love (for agapē in many contexts). The KJV's specific contribution was systematizing and harmonizing across the text while retaining Tyndale's core vocabulary wherever it was felicitous and precise.

Key KJV rendering decisions with doctrinal significance: “propitiation” (for hilastērion and hilasmos; Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2; 4:10) — a term that preserves the wrath-averting function of Christ's sacrifice, which “expiation” (the RSV's substitution) does not; “lovingkindness” (for Hebrew chesed) — a compound the KJV translators coined to capture the covenantal loyalty and tender affection that no single English word conveyed; “charity” (for agapē in 1 Corinthians 13 and elsewhere) — the Vulgate's caritas underlying the choice, emphasizing the giving rather than the feeling.

The KJV's second-person singular pronouns (thou, thee, thy, thine) were retained to distinguish the singular from the plural (“you/you all”) at a time when English was losing this distinction in common usage. This preserves exegetically significant distinctions: John 3:7 (“ye must be born again”) distinguishes the plural audience from the singular Nicodemus; Matt 26:64 (“thou hast said”) is singular to the high priest. Modern translations render these without distinction, losing exegetical texture the KJV preserved.

The KJV's influence on English hymnody is incalculable: the Psalms of Isaac Watts, Charles Wesley's hymns, the Baptist and Presbyterian traditions' psalmody, William Cowper's poems, and the entire Victorian and Edwardian hymn tradition are saturated with KJV vocabulary, making the Authorized Version's word-stock the primary linguistic medium through which English-speaking Christians have expressed their piety for four hundred years. Congregations that have shifted entirely to modern versions are not merely making a translation choice; they are severing themselves from a hymnodic and devotional tradition that assumes the KJV's specific lexical choices.

Key Scripture

Psalm 119:89 — "Forever, O LORD, Your word is settled in heaven."

Proverbs 30:5 — "Every word of God is pure; He is a shield to those who put their trust in Him."

Isaiah 40:8 — "The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God stands forever."

Matthew 24:35 — "Heaven and earth will pass away — but My words shall not pass away."

Modern Corruption

Dynamic-equivalence translation philosophy treats the KJV's lexical choices as obstacles to comprehension rather than as exegetically precise instruments; the “gender-inclusive” revision trend replaces masculine generic pronouns with plural constructions that lose the singular-plural distinctions the KJV preserved; both trends reduce precision in the service of accessibility, at the cost of doctrinal texture.

expand to see more

Dynamic-equivalence translation philosophy, articulated by Eugene Nida and applied in the New International Version, the Good News Bible, and subsequent translations, aims to produce the same effect in the modern reader that the original produced in the ancient reader — a goal that in practice produces simplified vocabulary, shorter sentences, and the replacement of technical theological terms with general equivalents. The substitution of “expiation” for “propitiation” in the RSV (1952) exemplifies the doctrinal cost: “expiation” (removing the guilt of sin) loses the wrath-averting dimension of hilaskomai that “propitiation” preserves. Modern readers are assumed to be unable to learn “propitiation” and understand it; the KJV translators assumed the opposite, and their assumption produced a more doctrinally precise English Christianity.

The gender-inclusive revision of biblical translations — replacing masculine generic pronouns and nouns with plurals or gender-neutral alternatives — was applied to the New International Version in the 2011 revision and to numerous other modern translations. The problem is not merely cultural: masculine generic language in the biblical text often carries specific singular-universal scope (“the one who does this will live”; “happy is the man who”) that the plural replacement (“those who do this will live”; “happy are those who”) loses. Beyond the grammatical loss, the revision accommodates a cultural pressure that the Reformed tradition has consistently identified as coming from the wrong direction: the translation is adjusted to suit a gender ideology that the text was never intended to accommodate.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Authorized Version's 1611 publication under King James I's commission; the translation stands in the lineage of Tyndale (1526), Coverdale (1535), Matthew (1537), Great Bible (1539), Geneva (1560), and Bishops' Bible (1568); its Jacobean English, Received Text base, and fifty-four-scholar translation committee produced the most influential English Bible in history.

expand to see more

Tyndale New Testament (1526) — the primary source of KJV vocabulary; William Tyndale's direct translation from Erasmus' Greek New Testament introduced passover, scapegoat, atonement, mercy seat, Jehovah, and longsuffering into English biblical vocabulary; the KJV retained approximately 80–90 percent of Tyndale's New Testament wording.

Textus Receptus (Received Text) — the Greek New Testament tradition underlying the KJV's New Testament; compiled from manuscripts available in Western Europe in the sixteenth century (principally Erasmus' editions, Stephanus' editions, and Beza's edition); the TR differs from the Nestle-Aland critical text used by most modern translations in approximately 2,000 places, most minor but a few exegetically significant.

Masoretic Text (MT) — the Hebrew text underlying the KJV's Old Testament; the Masoretes' vowel-pointed and cantillated manuscript tradition (principal manuscripts: Codex Leningradensis, Aleppo Codex); the KJV translators were also aware of the Septuagint and occasionally preferred its readings, though the MT governed their translation.

Elizabethan and Jacobean English — the stage of the English language in which the KJV was translated (1604–1611); its thou/thee singular and ye/you plural distinction was already becoming archaic in common speech, which is why the translators retained it — it preserved second-person number distinctions that contemporary speech was losing, serving exegesis over idiomatic accessibility.

Geneva Bible (1560) — the KJV's primary predecessor in common use; the translation of the English Protestant exiles in Geneva, it was the first English Bible with verse numbering, the first with Reformed marginal notes, and the one Shakespeare quoted; the KJV improved on the Geneva's text while eliminating its interpretive marginal notes, which King James' commission considered too Calvinist and politically charged.

Usage

"Congregations that worship from the KJV are not merely making a traditionalist choice; they are embedding their piety in a lexical tradition that has shaped four centuries of English-speaking Reformed and Baptist theological discourse — a tradition that connects the Sunday-morning congregation to Bunyan, Spurgeon, Lloyd-Jones, and every English-language Baptist and Presbyterian confession."

"The case for the KJV is not that it is inspired or that it is the only faithful translation; it is that its specific rendering choices preserve doctrinal texture (propitiation, justification, sanctification, lovingkindness, longsuffering) that simplified modern translations often flatten, and that pastors committed to theological precision will generally find the KJV's vocabulary a better instrument for doctrinal preaching."

"Learning the KJV's distinctive vocabulary is itself a form of biblical literacy that no other single act can replicate: the preacher or layperson who has memorized Scripture in the Authorized Version carries within them four centuries of theological distillation — the work of fifty-four scholars, the refinement of Tyndale's genius, and the literary achievement of English prose at its most precise and majestic."
